title: When was this file added — and who deleted the one I need?
summary: Trace a file's whole life: the commit that created it, the commits that changed it, and the commit that deleted it — then bring a deleted file back from the dead.
mental_model: `--diff-filter` narrows history to commits that Added, Deleted, Modified or Renamed a path. Add, delete and rename are the three events in a file's life, and each has a one-letter filter.

commit.message: Add v1 to v2 migration script

steps.title: Confirm the file is gone from the working tree
steps.why: It is not on disk and not in HEAD. Everything below happens in history, where it still exists — deleting a file never removes it from past commits.

steps.title: Search history for the path
steps.why: `log -- <path>` still finds it, because the path existed in past commits. Adding `--all` would search every branch too. Four commits touched this file across its life.

steps.title: Find the commit that created it
steps.why: `--diff-filter=A` keeps only commits where the path was Added. This is the answer to 'when did this get here and why', which is usually the real question behind 'what is this file'.

verify.label: exactly one commit added the file

steps.title: Find the commit that deleted it
steps.why: `--diff-filter=D` is the mirror image, and it is the one you reach for during an incident. Now you have a sha, an author and a message explaining the removal.

steps.title: Read the file as it was just before deletion
steps.why: The deleting commit does not contain the file — its parent does. `<sha>^` is that parent, and the caret is the single most useful character in git's revision syntax.
steps.expect: The full file, printed from history.

steps.title: Bring it back
steps.why: `restore --source` with that parent revision writes the file back into your working tree at its last known good state. No revert, no reset, no touching the six commits that came after.

verify.label: the deleted file is back, with its final content

steps.title: Commit the resurrection with an explanation
steps.why: A file coming back from the dead deserves a message saying why. Six months from now, `--diff-filter=A` will find this commit and the reader will get the whole story.
commands: git commit -m "Restore migration script: still needed for v1 customers"
steps.expect: Two 'added' events now — the original and the restoration.

verify.label: the deleted file was recovered in full
verify.hint: find the deleting commit with --diff-filter=D, restore from its parent with ^

verify.label: history records both the original add and the restoration
verify.hint: commit the restored file so the recovery is documented

verify.label: the deletion is still in history — you added to it, you did not rewrite it

pitfalls: `git log -- <deleted path>` needs the exact path as it was. If the file was renamed first, add `--follow` or search with `--diff-filter=R`.
The deleting commit does not contain the file. Always restore from `<sha>^`, never `<sha>`.
`--diff-filter` letters: A added, D deleted, M modified, R renamed, C copied. Lowercase excludes instead of includes.
On a merge commit, diff-filter results can be empty because git compares against the first parent by default.
